title: DND: Boosting Large Language Models with Dynamic Nested Depth
claim: Reasoning-critical tokens in a query and answer deserve extra computation, so a router re-feeds them through a layer again.
layout: Left QA text boxes, right stacked transformer layers; dotted arrows link them
description: The left side shows two rounded boxes. The top box holds a physics multiple-choice question about quantum state lifetimes and energy uncertainty, and the bottom box holds the start of the answer. The critical words and formulas are in red (E1, E2, lifetime, energy difference, ΔE ≈ ħ/(2Δt)). Dotted arrows lead from these boxes to the right side. The right side is a stack of three offset, rounded yellow panels labeled 'Shallow → Deep' with a gradient bar, which stand for layers. The front panel shows a row of token squares going into a 'Transformer Layer' (L_s), then a 'Linear Selection Router'. The router sends a few selected tokens, shown in red, into a second, red-outlined 'Transformer Layer' with a 'Share' label. A red double arrow marks 'Nested Depth'. The back panel is marked L_e. Red is the main accent color, and the eye goes first to the red text.
caption: DND Motivation. The tokens highlighted in red denote critical elements in the QA pair. We propose a strategy within the transformer layers to identify and allocate additional computation to these critical tokens. $L_s$ and $L_e$ indicate the starting and end layers that adopted this strategy.
abstract: We introduce Dynamic Nested Depth (DND), a novel method that improves performance for off-the-shelf LLMs by selecting critical tokens to reprocess in a nested depth manner. Specifically, at the end of the given transformer layer, DND identifies more critical tokens with a router and feeds them back for an extra round of processing, effectively ``reviewing" difficult tokens while avoiding redundant computation for easier ones. The dynamic selection mechanism is tailored for precise control via two novel strategies: a router controlling loss to enhance token selection distinguishability, and a threshold control scheme to ensure selection stability. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DND by directly integrating it into pre-trained dense and MoE models during a post-training phase. On diverse benchmarks, this approach boosts the performances of the dense Qwen3-1.7B by 1.88% and the MoE Qwen3-30B-A3B by 0.87%, all with a minimal parameter and computing increase.
